messages.content: Write about a startup talk given at a Seattle event in 2010, covering a three-part product philosophy: first, identify and care deeply about a real problem; second, release the smallest workable version of the solution instead of overbuilding, since you only learn by putting it in front of people; and third, focus on and genuinely care for the users because making consumer products is more like hosting a great gathering than engineering a machine. Include a brief note of thanks for the event and audience, mention that the slides summarize the talk, and end with a reflection on how many people helped along the way, plus an invitation to local engineers and builders to join in. Keep it around 260 words.

via slideshare.net

Thanks so much to Seattle 2.0 for having me here at StartupDay 2010. It seriously was a blast talking to so many excited entrepreneurs and pre-entrepreneurs.

Above are my slides from my talk. It's pretty straightforward, in as few words as possible:

- First, hate the problem. This means you really connect with something that SUCKS A LOT and you know is a real problem. Come on people, we work in tech. There are a lot of things that are terrible. PC LOAD LETTER, what the heck does that mean!?

- Second, ship the solution. The product. Get the smallest possible quantum and don't boil the ocean. You don't know whether your product is goodt il it's out there.

- Third, love your users. If you build it, they won't come. Building consumer web startups is absolutely not like building a car, but that's how we think about building them. It's logistics and technology and mechanisms. No, no, no. It's more like throwing a really awesome party. And nobody throws parties for people who they don't love.

So that's what I got in a nutshell. I can't believe how many people have helped us along the way (and we are so far from done!) but it feels great to be able to give back and help more people get to fulfill their dreams.

Seattle is probably the biggest collection of amazing software engineers and product creators outside of the Bay Area -- but they're all locked up in massive vaults called Microsoft and Amazon. Come on out guys, the water's fine.

title: Hate, Ship, Love: A Product-driven State of Mind (Seattle StartupDay 2010 talk I just gave today) - garry's posthaven

messages.content:
Write about the difference between science and reason as two ways of knowing: science as outward-facing, based on measurement, experiments, data, and repeatable results, and reason as inward-facing, based on mental models and deduction from an internal sense of what seems true. Include the idea that these correspond to two kinds of people or approaches, and then extend the comparison to business and product work by explaining how one camp emphasizes product intuition and building something people want, while another emphasizes metrics and analysis after launch.

Also cover the practical point that both approaches matter in startups: product sense helps you decide what to make in the first place, but analytics helps you learn whether it is working once it is in the world. Mention that the passage uses the contrast to argue these are different but complementary tools that are strongest when used together, and keep it to about 200 words.

Science is about the external world: measurement, controlled experiment, data collection, empiricism. It tests hypotheses against the hard reality of repeatable experiments with objectively measurable results. Those who practice it are called scientists or empiricists.

Reason, by contrast, is internally generated. It’s building mental models of the world, starting with your internal sense for what is right and pure, from which further truths can be deduced. Those who practice reason are called rationalists.

via adam.heroku.com

Adam Wiggins of Heroku breaks down science vs. reason and how it affects business decisions in a startup -- and I was struck by how there are similarly very entrenched camps that are highly product (PG / YC-style / build something people want) oriented vs. highly metrics (Paypal mafia / Andrew Chen / Slide+Zynga) oriented.

When you build a product, you've got to have a worldview on what people want and what is useful and good. That's product sense. But once it is out in the world, you need to iterate and use empiricism to understand how your creation is doing. That's analytics.

As with science and reason, product and metrics are distinct things that happen to be extra valuable when used in conjunction.

title: Science vs Reason is like Product Design vs Analytics - garry's posthaven

messages.content: Write about how humans constantly compare experiences to seek pleasure and avoid pain, using the idea that we learn from friends, family, and media before trying things ourselves. Include examples like asking about food, movies, or other recommendations, explain that watching stories lets us mentally experience others’ lives, and connect this to the brain’s ability to empathize through mirrored experiences; then argue that review sites, search engines, and the internet help people make better choices by sharing knowledge quickly, ending with a broader point about the long history of expanding human empathy through communication tools. Keep it to about 310 words.

As Freud pointed out, people spend a shocking amount of time in a continuous cycle seeking pleasure and avoiding pain. Our internal monologue is but a continuous questioning -- how am I doing, and what should I be doing next? When we meet with friends and family, in between the great stories and moments of laughter and levity-- we ask how they're doing, how that food is, what are you going to order, how was that movie, what's new, and so on.

In essence, when we ask each other how things were, we're comparing our experiences. How was that steak? Great? Awesome, I'm going to have that too. The Other Guys was a great movie? Sweet, I have to see it. It sucked? Thanks for letting me avoid that one. (It was awesome by the way)

Even when we watch movies, we experience, temporarily, the lives of others. We learn not just through the stories and experiences of people we know but also through the media we consume. Thanks to the amazing existence of mirror neurons, as we see and hear things happen to others, our brains fire up the same patterns they would had they happened directly to us.

As it turns out, our brains and minds are elaborate engines for processing information and experiences. That goes for everything from websites to a good meal at a restaurant. So it's natural that we want to avoid pain and seek pleasure through foreknowledge by people we trust.
But that's what Yelp is for. And the web. And Google. The arc of history is that of an ever-increasing amount of empathy -- and the web is merely the latest and greatest enabler in that. The beginning of this arc? Verbal language. Written language. Scrolls. Codexes. The printing press. Paperback books. Paperback computers. And now the infinitely vast and instantaneous Internet.

title: Yelp accelerates the pleasure principle, and that lets us all live better lives - garry's posthaven

messages.content: Write about how social sharing and review platforms may seem trivial at first, but actually help people make better choices and improve services. Explain that when information about movies, restaurants, and other experiences is easy to spread, good options get more attention, bad service is exposed, people are less likely to be cheated, and businesses are pushed to improve; include a simple example like dining out and getting a bad meal or service reviewed publicly, and end with the idea that each review or post contributes to a better system, in about 140 words.

At first blush, the now-dominant social way we use the Internet seems shallow. Who cares what movie so-and-so watched? Or that they ate at that fancy new restaurant and it sucked. Why should it appear on my Facebook feed at all? But we should care. We do care. It allows us to live better lives. If there is less friction in knowledge, then the good restaurants and the good movies get the attention they deserve. Bad service is penalized. People don't get ripped off so often. Because a durable public channel for feedback exists, restaurants and services can get better.

Less spit in coffee, more awesomeness. We each have a voice in this, and if we pay into the system, we help each other live better... One blog post or Yelp review at a time.

title: Yelp accelerates the pleasure principle, and that lets us all live better lives - garry's posthaven

messages.content: Write a passage about how many people are currently using a website and other hosted services, and how every visit creates either a good or bad experience. Explain that this applies to any consumer brand, from large companies to small local businesses, and argue that the goal should be to improve frequent interactions immediately rather than waiting for a perfect future, because delays mean more people keep having poor experiences. Also cover the idea that small annoyances can add up over time into a significant amount of frustration, and that designers, engineers, and product teams have a responsibility to reduce that pain and create better outcomes.

At this moment there are thousands of people connecting to this website and others that are hosted on Posterous. Each of those people comes away from that interaction with a positive or negative experience.

This is true for all websites and all consumer brand experiences actually... If you are Hertz, American Airlines, or even the corner coffee shop, there are experiences and interactions that happen with great frequency. Our challenge is to make as many of those experiences positive. Not tomorrow. Not next week. Now. Because it is easy to envision a distant future that is better. But until that future is realized, thousands or millions of other people will have to endure a bad experience before you can get your act together. They may be tiny grievances accumulated over hours and days, but in the meantime a better future is sitting in a Gantt chart or bug tracker or Excel spreadsheet someplace.

These are only the minor annoyances, though I'm sure there are a few major ones as well. But when you add it all up over time and frequency that is one heck of a lot of human pain. Luckily, it is within our hands as designers and engineers and experience creators to turn that pain into happiness. It is our job. We care and we are working on it. So should you.

title: Fix it now - garry's posthaven

messages.content: Write about a quirky grocery chain that feels more like a discovery experience than a routine place to shop, and explain how it mixes budget-friendly basics with unusual imported treats that shoppers can’t easily find elsewhere. Also note that a recent business article revealed the chain was sold to a German family behind a major supermarket business and that the company is expanding rapidly; mention that this surprising background and growth are worth highlighting in about 120 words.

It stocks its shelves with a winning combination of low-cost, yuppie-friendly staples (cage-free eggs and organic blue agave sweetener) and exotic, affordable luxuries -- Belgian butter waffle cookies or Thai lime-and-chili cashews -- that you simply can't find anyplace else.

via money.cnn.com

Trader Joe's is an amazing place, and with very little coverage. But Fortune does an admirable job of filling us in.

Did not realize that the store had been sold to a German family that is better known for a large German chain of supermarkets. And that they're expanding like mad. Good on them. They rock.
